Symptomatic human infection is caused by many viruses. The most
common are discussed here.
Norovirus
This icosahedral virus with a single-stranded RNA genome was previ-

environmental decontamination with alcohol-based hand sanitizers and

Whipple’s original case report described an individual with malabsorption, lymphadenopathy, and arthritis of undefined origin. Postmortem examination demonstrated the presence of foamy macrophages filled with gram-positive microbes. The organism was identified as an actino-mycete in 1992 and named Tropheryma whipplei. Clinical symptoms occur because bacteria-laden macrophages accumulate within the small intestinal lamina propria and mesenteric lymph nodes, causing lymphatic  obstruction.  Thus,  the  malabsorptive  diarrhea  of  Whipple disease is due to impaired lymph drainage.
MORPHOLOGY
The morphologic hallmark of Whipple disease is a dense accumulation of distended, foamy macrophages in the small intestinal lamina propria

(Fig. 17.33A). The macrophages contain periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)–positive, diastase-resistant granules that represent partially digested bacteria within lysosomes (Fig. 17.33B). Intact rod-shaped bacilli can also be identified by electron microscopy (Fig. 17.33C). A similar infiltrate of foamy macrophages is present in intestinal mycobacterial infections (Fig. 17.33D), and the organisms are PAS-positive in both diseases. The acid-fast stain can be helpful, since mycobacteria stain positively (Fig. 17.33E), while T. whipplei does not.
Villous  expansion  caused  by  dense  macrophage  infiltrates  imparts  a

“shaggy”  appearance  to  the  mucosal  surface.  Lymphatic  dilation  and mucosal lipid deposition produce endoscopically visible white to yellow mucosal plaques. In Whipple disease, bacteria-laden macrophages can accumulate within mesenteric lymph nodes, synovial membranes, cardiac valves, brain, and other sites.
Clinical Features

Whipple disease is most common in males of Northern European descent, particularly farmers and others with occupational exposure to soil or animals. While there is no consistent familial clustering, the rarity of infection despite a large number of healthy carriers suggests that genetic risk factors exist.

The clinical presentation of Whipple disease is usually a triad of diarrhea, weight loss, and arthralgia. Extraintestinal symptoms may precede malabsorption by months or years and include arthritis; arthralgia; fever; lymphadenopathy; and neurologic, cardiac, or pulmonary disease.
Viral Gastroenteritis
Symptomatic human infection is caused by many viruses. The most common are discussed here.
Norovirus

This icosahedral virus with a single-stranded RNA genome was previously known as Norwalk-like virus. With increasing use of the rotavirus vaccine, norovirus has become the most common cause of diarrhea worldwide, being responsible for ,20% of acute gastroenteritis
with diarrhea and vomiting and 50,000 pediatric deaths annually. In the United States norovirus outbreaks occur in the winter and affect
,20 million people annually.

Humans are the only known reservoir of norovirus. Fecal-oral transmission is responsible of most sporadic cases. Outbreaks spread easily within schools, hospitals, nursing homes, and other large groups in close quarters, such as on cruise ships. In these environments, vehicles for transmission  include  airborne  droplets,  environmental  surfaces,  and fomites. Enforcement of personal hygiene, enteric precautions, and regular

Norovirus infection in immunocompromised patients is a significant problem. Some data suggest that nearly 20% of patients on immunosuppression after renal transplantation or as treatment for graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation are infected with norovirus. Many of these patients are unable to clear the infection, experience chronic diarrhea, and shed infectious virus for up to 1 year.

Some individuals are naturally resistant to norovirus infection due to mutations that inactivate galactoside 2-alpha-L-fucosyltrans-ferase (FUT2), an enzyme that fucosylates proteins in the Golgi apparatus that are destined for the plasma membrane, including blood group antigens. These glycoproteins serve as binding sites for the virus, and in their absence cells cannot be infected. Approximately 20% of individuals of European and African descent are homozygous for these mutations. These individuals, termed nonsecretors, neither shed blood group antigens in saliva nor express them on epithelial cells at mucosal sites including the GI tract. In others, acquired immunity is difficult to achieve because there is a great diversity of norovirus strains, which limits cross protection, and because the viral genome regularly undergoes recombination that results in antigenic shifts. As a result, a new pandemic strain emerges every 2 to 4 years.
MORPHOLOGY

Morphologic changes are nonspecific but include mild villous shortening, epithelial vacuolization, crypt hypertrophy, and lamina propria infiltration by neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes (Fig. 17.34A). The microvillus brush border is also compromised, and reduced expression of digestive enzymes can lead to mild steatorrhea and carbohydrate malabsorption.

Children between 6 and 24 months of age are most vulnerable, probably because antibodies in breast milk confer protection during the first 6 months of life. Rotavirus vaccines are becoming widely used but are incompletely effective in under-resourced regions, possibly as a consequence of malnutrition. The WHO recommends that the first dose be given at 6 weeks of age.

Larvae can also form hepatic abscesses and cause pneumonitis. Diagnosis is usually made by detection of eggs in stool samples.
Strongyloides

The larvae of Strongyloides live in fecally contaminated ground soil and can penetrate unbroken skin. They migrate through the lungs, where they induce inflammatory infiltrates, and then reside in the intestine while  maturing  into  adult  worms.  Unlike  other  intestinal  worms, which require an ova or larval stage outside the human, the eggs of Strongyloides can hatch within the intestine and release larvae that penetrate the mucosa, causing autoinfection (see Fig. 17.34B). Hence, Strongyloides infection can persist for life, and immunosuppressed individuals  can  develop  overwhelming  autoinfection.  Strongyloides incite a strong tissue reaction and peripheral eosinophilia.
Necator duodenale and Ancylostoma duodenale

These hookworms infect 1 billion people worldwide and cause significant morbidity. Infection is initiated by larval penetration through the skin. After further development in the lungs, they migrate up the trachea and are swallowed. Worms attach to the duodenal mucosa, suck blood, and reproduce. This causes multiple superficial erosions, focal hemorrhage, inflammatory infiltrates, and, in chronic infection, iron deficiency anemia. Diagnosis can be made by detection of eggs in fecal smears.
Trichuris trichiura

Whipworms primarily infect young children. Like Enterobius vermicularis, T. trichiura does not penetrate the intestinal mucosa and rarely causes serious disease. Heavy infections may cause bloody diarrhea and rectal prolapse.
Enterobius vermicularis and Enterobius gregorii

These organisms, also known as pinworms, infect people in both high-resource and low-resource countries; over 1 billion are infected worldwide. E. vermicularis is the more common species, but E. gregorii has been reported in Europe, Africa, and Asia. Because they do not invade host  tissues  and  live  their  entire  life  within  the  intestinal  lumen, pinworms rarely cause serious illness. Infection is primarily by the fecal-oral route. Adult worms living in the intestine migrate to the anal orifice at night, where the female deposits eggs on the perirectal mucosa.  The  eggs  cause  irritation  and  rectal  and  perineal  pruritus.

Scratching leads to contamination of the fingers, which promotes human-to-human transmission. Both eggs and adult pinworms remain viable outside the body, and repeat infection is common. Diagnosis can be made by applying cellophane tape to the perianal skin and examining the tape under a microscope to identify eggs.
Schistosomiasis

This disease involving the intestines most commonly takes the form of adult worms residing within the mesenteric veins. Eggs are trapped within the mucosa and submucosa (Fig. 17.34C). The resulting immune reaction is often granulomatous and can cause bleeding and even obstruction. More details are presented in Chapter 8.

meat, or pork that contains encysted larvae. Release of the larva allows attachment to the intestinal mucosa through its head, or scolex. The

worm derives its nutrients from the food stream and enlarges by forma-
tion of egg-filled segments termed proglottids. Humans are usually in-
fected by a single worm, and since the worm does not penetrate the in-
testinal  mucosa,  peripheral  eosinophilia  does  not  generally  occur.
Nevertheless, the parasite burden can be staggering. Adult worms can
grow to many meters in length and shed large numbers of proglottids
and eggs into the feces. Clinical symptoms include abdominal pain, diar-
rhea, and nausea, but most cases are asymptomatic. Occasionally, D. la-
tum causes vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and megaloblastic anemia because it
competes with the host for dietary B₁₂. Identification of proglottids and
eggs in stools is the most efficient method of diagnosis.
Entamoeba histolytica
This protozoan causes amebiasis and is spread by fecal-oral transmis-
sion. E. histolytica infects approximately 500 million people in coun-
tries such as India, Mexico, and Colombia and causes 40 million cases
of dysentery and liver abscess annually. The cysts have a chitin wall that
is resistant to gastric acid, a characteristic that allows them to pass
through the stomach without harm. E. histolytica then colonizes the
epithelial surface of the colon and releases trophozoites, amoeboid
forms that reproduce under anaerobic conditions.
Amebiasis affects the cecum and ascending colon most often, but sig-
moid colon, rectum, and appendix can also be involved. Dysentery devel-
ops when the amoebas attach to the colonic epithelium, induce apoptosis,
invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria. The infection
results in recruitment of neutrophils, tissue damage, and formation of
flask-shaped ulcers with a narrow neck and broad base. Histologic diagno-
sis can be difficult because amoebas resemble macrophages in size and
appearance (Fig. 17.34D). Parasites penetrate splanchnic vessels and em-
bolize to the liver to produce abscesses in about 40% of patients with
amoebic dysentery. Amebic liver abscesses can exceed 10 cm in diameter
and have a scant inflammatory reaction at their margins and a shaggy fi-
brinous lining. The abscesses persist after the acute intestinal illness has
passed and may, rarely, reach the lung and the heart by direct extension.
Amoebas may also spread to the kidneys and brain via the bloodstream.
Individuals  with  amebiasis  may  present  with  abdominal  pain,
bloody diarrhea, or weight loss. Occasionally, acute necrotizing colitis
and megacolon occur; both are associated with significant mortality.
The parasites lack mitochondria or Krebs cycle enzymes and are thus
obligate fermenters of glucose. Metronidazole, which inhibits pyruvate
oxidoreductase, an enzyme required for fermentation, is the most
effective treatment for systemic disease.
Giardia lamblia
These organisms, also referred to as G. duodenalis or G. intestinalis,
were initially described by van Leeuwenhoek, the inventor of the mi-
croscope, who discovered the pathogen in his own stool. G. lamblia is
the most common parasitic pathogen in humans and is spread by
fecally contaminated water or food. Infection may occur after inges-
tion of as few as 10 cysts. Because cysts are resistant to chlorine, Giar-
dia are endemic in unfiltered public water supplies. They are also
common in rural streams, explaining infection in campers who use
these as a water source. Infection may occur by the fecal-oral route,
and because the cysts are stable, they may be accidentally swallowed
while swimming in contaminated water.
Giardia are flagellated protozoa that cause decreased expression of
brush-border enzymes, microvillous damage, and apoptosis of small
intestinal epithelial cells. Secretory IgA and mucosal IL-6 responses are
important  for  clearance  of  Giardia  infections.  Immunosuppressed,
agammaglobulinemic, or malnourished individuals are often severely
affected. Giardia can evade immune clearance through continuous
modification of their major surface antigen, variant surface protein,
and can persist for months or years, causing intermittent symptoms.
Giardia trophozoites can be identified in duodenal biopsies based on
their characteristic pear shape and the presence of two equally sized nu-
clei. Despite large numbers of trophozoites, some of which are tightly
bound to the brush border of villous enterocytes, there is no invasion, and
small intestinal morphology may be normal (Fig. 17.34E); villous blunt-
ing with increased numbers of intraepithelial lymphocytes and mixed
lamina propria inflammatory infiltrates can accompany heavy infections.
Giardiasis may be subclinical or accompanied by acute or chronic
diarrhea, malabsorption, and weight loss. Infection is usually docu-
mented by immunofluorescent detection of cysts in stool samples. Oral
antimicrobial therapy is effective, but recurrence is common. Infants
and young children, travelers, and immunocompromised patients have
an increased risk of severe disease.
Cryptosporidium
Like Giardia, cryptosporidia are an important cause of diarrhea world-
wide. They cause an acute, self-limited disease in both immunocom-
promised and immunologically normal hosts. Cryptosporidiosis also
causes persistent diarrhea in residents of under-resourced countries.
Oocysts are resistant to chlorine and may therefore persist in treated,
but unfiltered, water. Contaminated drinking water continues to be the
most common means of transmission. The largest documented out-
break, a result of inadequate water purification, occurred in 1993 in
Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and affected more than 400,000 people. Like
giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis is readily spread to water sport enthusi-
asts. Food-borne infection occurs less frequently.
Humans are infected by several different Cryptosporidium species,
including C. hominis and C. parvum. All go through an entire life cycle,
with asexual and sexual reproductive phases, in a single host. Once
ingested, as few as 10 encysted oocytes are sufficient to cause symp-
tomatic infection. Sporozoites are released following protease activa-
tion  by  gastric  acid.  They  are  motile  and  have  a  specialized
organelle that attaches to the brush border and causes changes in the
enterocyte cytoskeleton. These changes induce the enterocyte to engulf
the parasite, which takes up residence in an endocytic vacuole. Sodium
malabsorption,  chloride  secretion,  and  increased  tight  junction
permeability cause the nonbloody, watery diarrhea that ensues.
Mucosal histology is often only minimally altered, but persistent
cryptosporidiosis  in  children  and  heavy  infection  in  immunosup-
pressed patients can result in villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and
inflammatory infiltrates. Although the sporozoite is intracellular, it
appears, by light microscopy, to sit on top of the epithelial apical mem-
brane (Fig. 17.34F). Organisms are typically most concentrated in the
terminal ileum and proximal colon, but can be present throughout the
gut, biliary tract, and even the respiratory tract of immunodeficient
hosts. Diagnosis is based on finding oocysts in the stool.
KEY CONCEPTS
Infectious Enterocolitis
•  V. cholerae secrete a preformed toxin that causes massive chloride secre-
tion. Water follows the resulting osmotic gradient, leading to high volume
secretory diarrhea.
•  C. jejuni is the most common bacterial enteric pathogen in high-income
countries and also causes traveler’s diarrhea. Most isolates are noninvasive.
•  Salmonella and Shigella spp. are invasive and associated with exudative
bloody diarrhea (dysentery).
•  Salmonella enteritidis infection is a common cause of food poisoning.
•  S. typhi cause systemic disease (typhoid fever).
•  Pseudomembranous colitis is often triggered by antibiotic therapy. The re-
sponsible organism, C. difficile, releases toxins that disrupt epithelial function
and induce an inflammatory response that includes characteristic volcano-like
neutrophil eruptions that spread to form mucopurulent pseudomembranes.

This protozoan causes amebiasis and is spread by fecal-oral transmission. E. histolytica infects approximately 500 million people in countries such as India, Mexico, and Colombia and causes 40 million cases

of dysentery and liver abscess annually. The cysts have a chitin wall that is resistant to gastric acid, a characteristic that allows them to pass through the stomach without harm. E. histolytica then colonizes the epithelial surface of the colon and releases trophozoites, amoeboid forms that reproduce under anaerobic conditions.

Amebiasis affects the cecum and ascending colon most often, but sigmoid colon, rectum, and appendix can also be involved. Dysentery develops when the amoebas attach to the colonic epithelium, induce apoptosis,

invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria. The infection results in recruitment of neutrophils, tissue damage, and formation of flask-shaped ulcers with a narrow neck and broad base. Histologic diagnosis can be difficult because amoebas resemble macrophages in size and appearance (Fig. 17.34D). These organisms, also referred to as G. duodenalis or G. intestinalis, were initially described by van Leeuwenhoek, the inventor of the microscope, who discovered the pathogen in his own stool. G. lamblia is the most common parasitic pathogen in humans and is spread by

fecally contaminated water or food. Infection may occur after ingestion of as few as 10 cysts. Because cysts are resistant to chlorine, Giardia are endemic in unfiltered public water supplies. They are also

• Norovirus is a common cause of self-limited diarrhea in adults and children.
It spreads from person to person in sporadic cases and via contaminated
water in epidemics.
• Rotavirus causes severe childhood diarrhea and significant mortality worldwide. Widespread vaccination has reduced the incidence of rotavirus infection.
• Epithelial expressions of proteins that serve as SARS-CoV-2 receptors may
explain gastrointestinal symptoms in ,50% of patients with COVID-19.
• Parasitic and protozoal infections affect more than one-half of the world’s
population on a chronic or recurrent basis. Each parasite has a distinctive
life cycle and tissue reaction. Those that invade are typically associated
with tissue and systemic eosinophilia.
IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is characterized by chronic, relapsing
abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits. Despite real
symptoms, endoscopic and microscopic evaluations are normal in IBS
patients. Thus, the diagnosis depends on clinical symptoms and functional testing. It should be recognized that IBS is a syndrome consisting
of a spectrum of multiple illnesses, and that multiple illnesses may fall
under this broad descriptor. IBS is currently divided into diarrhea-predominant, constipation-predominant, and mixed subtypes.
Pathogenesis
The pathogenesis of IBS remains poorly defined, although there is
clearly interplay between psychologic stressors, diet, perturbation of
the gut microbiome, increased enteric sensory responses to GI stimuli,
and abnormal GI motility. For example, patients with constipation-predominant or diarrhea-predominant IBS tend to have decreased or
increased colonic contractions and transit rates, respectively. Excess
bile acid synthesis or bile acid malabsorption has been identified as
one cause of diarrhea-predominant IBS, likely due to the effects of bile
acids on intestinal motility and epithelial ion transport.
Other data link disturbances in enteric nervous system function
to IBS, suggesting a role for defective brain-gut axis signaling. Consistent with this, deep sequencing and genome-wide association
studies have linked several candidate genes to IBS including serotonin reuptake transporters, cannabinoid receptors, and TNF-related
inflammatory mediators. Further, 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are
effective in many cases of diarrhea-predominant IBS. Opioids and
psychoactive drugs with anticholinergic effects are also used to treat
diarrhea-predominant IBS.
A separate group of IBS patients relate onset to a bout of infectious
gastroenteritis, suggesting that immune activation or, alternatively, a
shift in the gut microbiome may trigger disease.
Clinical Features
The peak prevalence of IBS is between 20 and 40 years of age, and there
is a significant female predominance. Variability in diagnostic criteria
makes it difficult to establish the incidence, but most authors report a
prevalence in high-income countries of between 5% and 10%. IBS is
presently diagnosed using clinical criteria that require the occurrence
of abdominal pain or discomfort at least 3 days per month over
3 months with improvement following defecation and a change
in stool frequency or form. Other causes, such as enteric infection or
inflammatory bowel disease, must be excluded.
INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition comprised
of two disorders, ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. Descriptions of
ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease date back to antiquity and at least
the sixteenth century, respectively, but it took modern microbiologic
techniques to exclude more common infectious etiologies for these
diseases. As will be discussed later, however, luminal microbiota likely
play an important role in IBD pathogenesis.
The distinction between ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease is
based on the distribution of affected sites (Fig. 17.35) and the morphologic expression of disease (Table 17.8) at those sites. In simplest terms,
ulcerative colitis involves only the colon and rectum and is limited
to the mucosa and submucosa. In contrast, Crohn disease, which
was previously termed ileal enteritis due to frequent involvement of
the ileum, may involve any area of the GI tract and is typically
transmural.

Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease most frequently present in the
teenage years and early 20s but can develop at any age. IBD is most
common among people of European descent, and in the United States

• Norovirus is a common cause of self-limited diarrhea in adults and children.

life cycle and tissue reaction. Those that invade are typically associated
with tissue and systemic eosinophilia.

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is characterized by chronic, relapsing
abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits. Despite real
symptoms, endoscopic and microscopic evaluations are normal in IBS
patients. Thus, the diagnosis depends on clinical symptoms and func-

of a spectrum of multiple illnesses, and that multiple illnesses may fall
under this broad descriptor. IBS is currently divided into diarrhea-pre-
dominant, constipation-predominant, and mixed subtypes.
Pathogenesis
The pathogenesis of IBS remains poorly defined, although there is
clearly interplay between psychologic stressors, diet, perturbation of
the gut microbiome, increased enteric sensory responses to GI stimuli,
and abnormal GI motility. For example, patients with constipation-
predominant or diarrhea-predominant IBS tend to have decreased or
increased colonic contractions and transit rates, respectively. Excess
bile acid synthesis or bile acid malabsorption has been identified as
one cause of diarrhea-predominant IBS, likely due to the effects of bile
acids on intestinal motility and epithelial ion transport.
Other data link disturbances in enteric nervous system function
to IBS, suggesting a role for defective brain-gut axis signaling. Con-
sistent with this, deep sequencing and genome-wide association
studies have linked several candidate genes to IBS including sero-
tonin reuptake transporters, cannabinoid receptors, and TNF-related
inflammatory mediators. Further, 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are
effective in many cases of diarrhea-predominant IBS. Opioids and
psychoactive drugs with anticholinergic effects are also used to treat
diarrhea-predominant IBS.
A separate group of IBS patients relate onset to a bout of infectious
gastroenteritis, suggesting that immune activation or, alternatively, a
shift in the gut microbiome may trigger disease.

The peak prevalence of IBS is between 20 and 40 years of age, and there

3 months with improvement following defecation and a change

occurs three to five times more often among eastern European (Ashke-

limit mucosal immune responses. This in turn allows some mucosa-

added to processed foods induce low-grade mucosal damage that pre-
disposes to IBD.
Pathogenesis
IBD results from a combination of abnormalities in immune regula-
tion, host-microbe interactions, and epithelial functions in genetically
susceptible individuals (Fig. 17.36).
Genetics.  Over 200 IBD-associated risk alleles have been identified,
but these account for less than 20% of disease risk in Crohn disease and
make even smaller contributions to ulcerative colitis. For example, in
European populations, NOD2, which encodes an intracellular sensor of
muramyl dipeptide, a bacterial cell wall component, is most strongly
associated with Crohn disease. Yet, the three major NOD2 risk alleles
are present in only ,30% of Crohn disease patients versus 5% of
which can be regulated by many cytokines. IL, Interleukin; TNF, tumor

healthy individuals. Moreover, individuals with one risk allele have
only a ,five-fold increased Crohn disease risk. Even those in whom
both copies of NOD2 are risk alleles, Crohn disease risk is increased
only ,20-fold. In addition, both frequencies and risk associations of
NOD2 and other IBD-associated loci vary widely across populations;
for example, NOD2 risk alleles are rare in Asian populations. Thus, IBD
is best understood as a polygenic disorder in which the accumulated
effects of multiple polymorphisms impact disease susceptibility. Con-
sistent with this, studies assessing all IBD genetic associations in ag-
gregate suggested some genotype-phenotype associations, including

behavior in Crohn disease, and extent of colonic involvement in ulcer-
ative colitis.

Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, and ,30% have indistinguishable
effect sizes in the two diseases. Two notable exceptions to this general-
ization are NOD2 and PTPN22 variants that increase Crohn disease
risk but are protective in ulcerative colitis. Interestingly, these genes are
also among the ,10% of IBD-associated polymorphisms that involve
coding sequences. Another ,30% of IBD loci are in regulatory regions
of genes, but neither coding nor gene expression changes are present
in over 50% of IBD-associated loci.
Despite some differences, the extensive overlap of Crohn disease
and ulcerative colitis genetic risk factors suggests that nearly all mecha-
nisms involved in one disease have a role in the other. When assessed
as clusters, IBD-associated genes are most closely linked to signaling in

IBD risk alleles overlap with those associated with other immune-me-
diated diseases, including type I diabetes, ankylosing spondylitis and
psoriasis. In most cases, specific polymorphisms have consistent effects
across diseases, but some that are associated with increased IBD risk are
protective in other diseases or vice versa.
A notable exception to the polygenic nature of IBD is very early
onset IBD (so-called infantile colitis), which can be monogenic, with
mutations of IL10 and the genes encoding the IL-10 receptor constitu-
ents IL10RA and IL10RB being the most common. Of the over 100
genes associated with monogenic IBD, the majority encode proteins
expressed in T cells and phagocytes. A smaller group of genes encode
epithelial cell proteins that contribute to epithelial barrier function,
intercellular adhesion, brush border digestion, ion and solute trans-
port, mucin secretion, and Paneth cell secretion of antimicrobial pep-
tides. Other mutations that cause monogenic IBD affect widely ex-
pressed genes involved in NOD signaling, NF-κB signaling, epithelial
death and survival, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (i.e., the
unfolded protein response). As might be expected, both functional and
genetic data implicate all these cell type specific and ubiquitous pro-
cesses in polygenic IBD.
Mucosal Immunity.  Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are both
characterized by mixed inflammatory reactions marked by activation of
Th17 and Th1 cells as well as more limited Th2 cell activation, particu-
larly in ulcerative colitis. Consistent with this, all current IBD therapies,
from corticosteroids to biologics, target the immune system; the effica-
cies of specific agents are generally similar in Crohn disease and ulcer-
ative colitis. Anti-TNF therapies are effective in IBD, presumably by
inhibiting inflammation Up to 50% of patients ultimately become unre-
sponsive to their first anti-TNF biologic. Some of these patients respond
to other anti-TNF biologics, but they may also be treated with other
biologics, including anti-IL-12/23p40 antibodies, which inhibit the ac-
tivation of Th1 and Th17 cells, and anti-IL-23, which inhibits Th17 cells.
In addition to biologic therapies, cytokine signaling has been targeted
in IBD using JAK inhibitors. Finally, disruption of lymphocyte traffick-
ing using anti-a4- or anti-a4b7-integrin antibodies or sphingosine-
1-phosphate receptor antagonists has proven effective in IBD. In sum-
mary, characterization of immune mechanisms of IBD have led to, and
been validated by, targeted therapies, but substantial gaps in our under-
standing of IBD immunopathogenesis remain.
Autophagy and Cellular Stress Responses.  Genetic associations as
well as molecular analyses indicate that defects in autophagy and cel-
lular stress responses contribute to IBD pathogenesis. The most stud-
ied of these genes include ATG16L1 and IRGM, both of which are in-
volved  in  autophagosome  formation.  Autophagy  is  a  normal
homeostatic mechanism that eliminates damaged organelles and is a
means of clearing sources of reactive oxygen species and intracellular
pathogens. The ATG16L1 mutation that is linked to Crohn disease
promotes  degradation  of  the  autophagy-related  protein  ATG16L1,
thereby limiting autophagy. The precise pathways by which loss of
ATG16L1 function leads to disease are still being defined, but it is
noteworthy that Paneth cell granules, which contain antibacterial pep-
tides that are released into the crypt lumen, are structurally and func-
tionally abnormal in patients with ATG16L1 defects.
Epithelial Barrier Dysfunction.  Partial loss of the intestinal epi-
thelial barrier, which limits interactions between the luminal milieu
and the mucosal immune system, has also been linked to IBD. Re-
sults are clearest in Crohn disease, where the ,10% of healthy rela-
tives of those with Crohn disease with modest barrier loss are at
greater risk of developing IBD than are healthy relatives without

barrier loss. Similarly, barrier loss during remission is associated
with relapse of active Crohn disease. Finally, preclinical data indi-
cate that barrier restoration can attenuate experimental IBD sever-
ity. Thus, compromise of a range of epithelial functions contributes
to IBD pathogenesis. No epithelial-targeted therapies are currently
available.
Host-Microbial Interactions.  The gut microbiome, composed of
bacteria, fungi, and viruses, and its role in IBD have been the subject
of intense investigation over the last decade. The microbiome is popu-
lated by a small number of species at birth and evolves to become a far
more complex ecosystem with many more species appearing after
weaning and through childhood. Patients with IBD often have shifts
in microbial populations and reduced species diversity, called dysbio-
sis. Although dysbiosis is often established at disease presentation, it
is difficult to differentiate between microbial changes that trigger
disease and those that are caused by disease. Unregulated immune
responses to bacterial species in the microbiome have been postulated
to underlie IBD, but neither the microbial triggers nor the specific
type of immune dysregulation have been defined. Recent studies have
focused on understanding the metabolites generated by microbes and
how these may impact immune and epithelial function, and to use
this knowledge to develop new therapies.
Crohn Disease
The eponym Crohn disease is based on a 1932 publication, but the
entity  was  described  centuries  earlier.  For  example,  Louis  XIII  of
France (1601–1643) experienced relapsing bloody diarrhea, fever, rec-
tal abscess, small intestinal and colonic ulcers, and fistulae beginning
at age 20 years, all of which are classic features of Crohn disease.
MORPHOLOGY
Crohn disease may occur in any area of the GI tract but most commonly
involves the terminal ileum, ileocecal valve, and cecum. Disease is limited to
the small intestine in about 40% of cases; the small intestine and colon are
both involved in 30% of patients; the remainder have only colonic involvement.
Pancolitis can be difficult to distinguish from ulcerative colitis. The presence of
multiple, separate, sharply delineated areas of disease, resulting in skip
lesions, is characteristic, and when present, differentiates Crohn disease
from ulcerative colitis. The presence of strictures, which occur commonly in
Crohn disease but only rarely in long-standing ulcerative colitis, may also be
helpful in diagnoses (Fig. 17.37A).
The earliest lesion of Crohn disease, the aphthous ulcer, may progress, and
multiple lesions often coalesce into elongated, serpentine ulcers oriented along
the long axis of the bowel (Fig. 17.37B). Edema and loss of the normal mucosal
folds are also common. Ulceration with sparing of interspersed mucosa, a result
of the patchy distribution of Crohn disease, can create an irregular, cobble-
stone appearance of the mucosa (see Fig. 17.37B). Fissures frequently develop
and may extend deeply to become peritoneal abscesses and perforation sites
(Fig. 17.37C). Alternatively, fissures may become fistula tracts between loops of
bowel or intestine and urinary bladder, vagina, or abdominal or perianal skin.
The intestinal wall is thickened and rubbery as a consequence of transmural
edema, inflammation, submucosal fibrosis, and hypertrophy of the muscularis
propria, all of which contribute to stricture formation (see Fig. 17.37A). In cases
with extensive transmural disease, mesenteric adipose tissue frequently ex-
tends over the serosal surface (creeping fat) (Fig. 17.37D).
The microscopic features of active Crohn disease include abundant neutro-
phils that infiltrate and damage crypt epithelium. Clusters of neutrophils within

A notable exception to the polygenic nature of IBD is very early onset IBD (so-called infantile colitis), which can be monogenic, with mutations of IL10 and the genes encoding the IL-10 receptor constituents IL10RA and IL10RB being the most common. Of the over 100 genes associated with monogenic IBD, the majority encode proteins expressed in T cells and phagocytes. A smaller group of genes encode epithelial cell proteins that contribute to epithelial barrier function,

intercellular adhesion, brush border digestion, ion and solute transport, mucin secretion, and Paneth cell secretion of antimicrobial peptides. Other mutations that cause monogenic IBD affect widely expressed genes involved in NOD signaling, NF-κB signaling, epithelial

death and survival, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (i.e., the unfolded protein response). As might be expected, both functional and genetic data implicate all these cell type specific and ubiquitous processes in polygenic IBD.

Mucosal Immunity. Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are both characterized by mixed inflammatory reactions marked by activation of Th17 and Th1 cells as well as more limited Th2 cell activation, particularly in ulcerative colitis. Consistent with this, all current IBD therapies,

from corticosteroids to biologics, target the immune system; the effica-cies of specific agents are generally similar in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Anti-TNF therapies are effective in IBD, presumably by

inhibiting inflammation Up to 50% of patients ultimately become unresponsive to their first anti-TNF biologic. Some of these patients respond to other anti-TNF biologics, but they may also be treated with other biologics, including anti-IL-12/23p40 antibodies, which inhibit the activation of Th1 and Th17 cells, and anti-IL-23, which inhibits Th17 cells.

In addition to biologic therapies, cytokine signaling has been targeted in IBD using JAK inhibitors. Finally, disruption of lymphocyte trafficking using anti-a4- or anti-a4b7-integrin antibodies or sphingosine-

1-phosphate receptor antagonists has proven effective in IBD. In summary, characterization of immune mechanisms of IBD have led to, and been validated by, targeted therapies, but substantial gaps in our understanding of IBD immunopathogenesis remain.

Autophagy and Cellular Stress Responses. Genetic associations as

well as molecular analyses indicate that defects in autophagy and cellular stress responses contribute to IBD pathogenesis. The most studied of these genes include ATG16L1 and IRGM, both of which are involved in autophagosome formation. Autophagy is a normal

homeostatic mechanism that eliminates damaged organelles and is a means of clearing sources of reactive oxygen species and intracellular pathogens. The ATG16L1 mutation that is linked to Crohn disease promotes degradation of the autophagy-related protein ATG16L1, thereby limiting autophagy. The precise pathways by which loss of ATG16L1 function leads to disease are still being defined, but it is noteworthy that Paneth cell granules, which contain antibacterial peptides that are released into the crypt lumen, are structurally and functionally abnormal in patients with ATG16L1 defects.

Results are clearest in Crohn disease, where the ,10% of healthy relatives of those with Crohn disease with modest barrier loss are at greater risk of developing IBD than are healthy relatives without

barrier loss. Similarly, barrier loss during remission is associated

with relapse of active Crohn disease. Finally, preclinical data indicate that barrier restoration can attenuate experimental IBD severity. Thus, compromise of a range of epithelial functions contributes

to IBD pathogenesis. No epithelial-targeted therapies are currently available.

Host-Microbial Interactions. The gut microbiome, composed of bacteria, fungi, and viruses, and its role in IBD have been the subject of intense investigation over the last decade. The microbiome is populated by a small number of species at birth and evolves to become a far more complex ecosystem with many more species appearing after weaning and through childhood. Patients with IBD often have shifts in microbial populations and reduced species diversity, called dysbiosis. Although dysbiosis is often established at disease presentation, it is difficult to differentiate between microbial changes that trigger disease and those that are caused by disease. Unregulated immune responses to bacterial species in the microbiome have been postulated to underlie IBD, but neither the microbial triggers nor the specific type of immune dysregulation have been defined. Recent studies have focused on understanding the metabolites generated by microbes and how these may impact immune and epithelial function, and to use this knowledge to develop new therapies.

Clinical Features
The clinical manifestations of Crohn disease are extremely variable. In most
patients, disease begins with intermittent attacks of relatively mild diarrhea,
abdominal pain, and fever. Approximately 20% of patients present acutely
with right lower quadrant pain, fever, and bloody diarrhea that may mimic
acute appendicitis or bowel perforation. Periods of active disease are typi-
cally interrupted by asymptomatic periods that last for weeks to many
months. Disease reactivation can be associated with a variety of external
triggers, including physical or emotional stress, specific dietary items, and
cigarette smoking. The latter is a strong risk factor for development of
Crohn disease, and in some cases, disease onset is associated with initiation
of smoking. Unfortunately, smoking cessation does not result in disease
remission. Intestinal barrier loss, which is present in ,10% of healthy first-
degree relatives of Crohn disease patients, is another risk factor for disease
development. Similarly, barrier dysfunction during remission is a marker of
impending relapse in those with established Crohn disease.
Iron deficiency anemia due to blood loss may develop in individuals
with colonic disease, while extensive small bowel disease may result in
protein loss sufficient to cause hypoalbuminemia and malabsorption of
nutrients, vitamin B₁₂, and bile salts. Fibrosing strictures, particularly of
the terminal ileum, are common and require surgical resection. Disease
often recurs at the site of anastomosis and necessitates additional resec-
tions within 10 years in up to 40% of patients. Bowel preservation is,
therefore, an important consideration when planning resections. As
discussed above, therapies focus on immunosuppression or immuno-
modulation  and  include  antiinflammatory  agents  (e.g.,  salicylates);
immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., corticosteroids); and biologic therapies
discussed earlier. Some current efforts aim to develop personalized
treatment algorithms based on clinical phenotype with genetic, im-
mune and microbiome data.
Crohn disease patients often have anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae anti-
bodies, which are typically absent in ulcerative colitis. Other manifesta-
tions of Crohn disease include cutaneous nodules formed by granulomas,
uveitis, migratory polyarthritis, sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis, ery-
thema nodosum, and clubbing of the fingertips, any of which may pre-
cede clinically evident intestinal disease. Crohn disease patients are also
at increased risk of developing pericholangitis and primary sclerosing
cholangitis, although the association is much stronger in ulcerative colitis
(see later and Chapter 18). As discussed later, risk of colonic adenocarci-
noma is increased in patients with long-standing colonic disease.
Ulcerative Colitis
Ulcerative colitis is closely related to Crohn disease, but intestinal
involvement is continuous and limited to the colon and rectum.
Although the implication for the pathogenesis is unclear, it is notable
that up to 75% of ulcerative colitis patients, but only ,10% of those
with Crohn disease, have perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic anti-
bodies (p-ANCA). Extraintestinal manifestations of ulcerative colitis
overlap with those of Crohn disease and include migratory polyarthri-
tis, sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis, uveitis, and skin lesions, but
neither intestinal nor extraintestinal granulomas are present. As noted
above, risk of primary sclerosing cholangitis is markedly increased in
ulcerative colitis and affects ,5% of patients (Chapter 18). Conversely,
the majority of those with primary sclerosing cholangitis also have
ulcerative colitis. The long-term outlook for ulcerative colitis patients
depends on the severity of active disease and disease duration. In gen-
eral, therapies, including anti-TNF antibodies, that are effective in
Crohn disease are also effective in ulcerative colitis.

Grossly, ulcerative colitis always involves the rectum and extends proximally in
a continuous fashion to involve part or all of the colon. Disease of the entire
colon is termed pancolitis (Fig. 17.39A). Limited distal disease may be referred

ative proctosigmoiditis. The small intestine is not affected, although mild
mucosal inflammation of the distal ileum, termed backwash ileitis, may be
present in severe cases of pancolitis. Although there are no skip lesions, focal
appendiceal or cecal inflammation, termed a cecal red spot, may be present
in left-sided ulcerative colitis.

in medical management. Although colectomy cures intestinal disease
in ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations may persist.

been hypothesized that enteritis triggers mucosal immune activation and

One of the most feared long-term complications of ulcerative colitis
and colonic Crohn disease is the development of neoplasia. The risk
of cancer is related to several factors:
•  Duration of the disease. Risk increases sharply 8 to 10 years after
disease onset.
•  Extent of the disease. Patients with pancolitis are at greater risk than
those with only left-sided disease. Crohn disease patients without
colonic involvement are not at increased risk.
•  Nature of the inflammatory response. Greater frequency and severity
of active inflammation (characterized by the presence of neutrophils)
confers increased risk.
To facilitate early detection of neoplasia, patients are typically
enrolled in surveillance programs approximately 8 years after diag-
nosis of IBD. The major exception to this is patients with IBD and
primary sclerosing cholangitis, who have a greater risk of develop-
ing cancer and are generally enrolled for surveillance at the time of
diagnosis.
The goal of surveillance biopsies is to identify dysplastic epithe-
lium, which is a precursor of colitis-associated carcinoma. Dysplasia
can develop in flat areas of mucosa that are not grossly recognized as
abnormal.  High-resolution  endoscopes  and  specialized  endoscopic
techniques, including chromoendoscopy, have helped target biopsies
toward areas suspicious for dysplasia, but multiple surveillance biop-
sies and histological examination are still required. IBD-associated
dysplasia  is  classified  histologically  as  low  grade  or  high  grade
(Fig. 17.41A,B) and may be multifocal. High-grade dysplasia may be
associated with invasive carcinoma at the same site (Fig. 17.41C) or
elsewhere in the colon and therefore often prompts colectomy. Low-
grade dysplasia may be followed closely with frequent endoscopic
surveillance, but colectomy is also common, particularly when multi-
ple foci of flat (nonpolypoid) dysplasia are present, in those with exten-
sive or long-standing disease, and in older patients. Cases of invasive
adenocarcinoma beneath superficial areas with only low-grade dyspla-
sia have been reported. IBD patients are susceptible to sporadic adeno-
mas, which can be difficult or impossible to differentiate from polypoid
foci of IBD-associated dysplasia. Fortunately, when solitary, polypoid
dysplastic lesions in the absence of flat dysplasia can often be managed
by endoscopic resection and careful follow-up.

phocytic colitis is histologically similar, but the subepithelial collagen
layer  is  of  normal  thickness  and  the  increase  in  intraepithelial

Graft-Versus-Host Disease
Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs following allogeneic hema-
topoietic stem cell transplantation. The small bowel and colon are in-
volved in most cases. Although graft-versus-host disease is secondary
to donor T cells targeting antigens on the recipient’s GI epithelial cells,
the lamina propria lymphocytic infiltrate is typically sparse. Epithelial
apoptosis, particularly of crypt cells, is the most common histologic
finding. The crypts may be completely destroyed in severe cases. Intes-
tinal graft-versus-host disease often presents with watery diarrhea that
may become bloody in severe cases.
Apoptotic Enterocolitis
Apoptotic enterocolitis is characterised by an increase in the num-
ber of apoptotic cells in the GI epithelium stemming from a myriad
of conditions. Enterocolitis and diarrhea are becoming increasingly
common in oncology patients treated with immune checkpoint in-
hibitors. In some cases, disease severity requires discontinuation of
treatment. The most common morphology associated within immune
checkpoint  inhibitor-induced  enterocolitis,  epithelial  apoptosis,  is
similar to graft-versus-host disease. Consistent with this, although
incompletely defined, the mechanisms of checkpoint inhibitor–in-
duced enterocolitis likely overlap, at least partially, with those of
graft-versus-host disease. Other forms of apoptotic enteritis and
colitis are associated with treatment with the immunosuppressive
agent mycophenolate mofetil.
SIGMOID DIVERTICULAR DISEASE
Diverticular disease is due to pseudodiverticular outpouchings of
the colonic mucosa and submucosa. Unlike true congenital divertic-
ula, such as Meckel diverticulum, colonic diverticula are acquired and
do not involve all layers of the bowel wall. They are rare in persons
younger than age 30 years, but the prevalence approaches 50% in West-
ern adult populations older than age 60 years. Diverticulosis is less
common in Japan as well as under-resourced countries, probably be-
cause of dietary differences.
Pathogenesis
Colonic diverticula are the product of the unique structure of the muscu-
laris propria and elevated intraluminal pressure. There are focal disconti-
nuities in the inner circular muscle layer at sites where nerves and arterial
vasa recta penetrate it. In the small intestine, these gaps are reinforced by
the external longitudinal layer of the muscularis propria. In contrast, the
outer muscle layer of the colon is gathered into three bands, the taeniae
coli, resulting in unreinforced sites where nerves and arteries cross the
inner layer of the muscularis propria. Increased intraluminal pressure can
cause the mucosa to herniate through the muscularis propria at these
unreinforced sites. This is most prominent in the sigmoid colon, where
exaggerated  peristaltic  contractions  occur,  particularly  in  association
with low-fiber diets that lead to reduced stool bulk. As a result, diverticula
are typically most common in the sigmoid colon in Western populations,
whereas they tend to occur in the right colon in Asian and African popu-
lations. Diverticular inflammation, which may be caused by obstruction
of the orifice, defines diverticulitis.
MORPHOLOGY
Colonic diverticula are 0.5 to 1 cm diameter flask-like outpouchings that are
uniformly spaced, reflecting the regular distribution of penetrating nerves and
arteries (Fig. 17.43A). The diverticular wall is formed by the mucosa, including
the muscularis mucosae, and separated from the serosal surface by a thin
layer of subserosal adipose tissue, sometimes in association with compressed
submucosa or attenuated muscularis propria. Inflammation within this narrow
region can therefore extend to cause serositis, and mucosal injury can result
in perforation, development of pericolonic abscesses, sinus tracts, and perito-
nitis. Hypertrophy of the inner circular layer of the muscularis propria is com-
monly associated with diverticulosis.
Clinical Features
Most  individuals  with  diverticular  disease  remain  asymptomatic
throughout their lives. However, about 20% develop manifestations
such as intermittent cramping, continuous lower abdominal discom-
fort, constipation, distention, or a sensation of never being able to
completely empty the rectum. Patients sometimes experience alternat-
ing constipation and diarrhea that mimics IBS. Whether a high-fiber
diet prevents or protects against diverticulitis is unclear, but diets
supplemented  with  fiber  may  provide  symptomatic  improvement.
Even when diverticulitis occurs, it most often resolves spontaneously.
Surgical intervention is generally reserved for those with severe or re-
current diverticulitis.

Most individuals with diverticular disease remain asymptomatic throughout their lives. Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The small bowel and colon are involved in most cases. Although graft-versus-host disease is secondary

KEY CONCEPTS
Enterocolitis and Related Disorders
•  Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is an umbrella term for ulcerative colitis
and Crohn disease. Indeterminate colitis is reserved for the few cases of
IBD  without  definitive  features  of  either  ulcerative  colitis  or  Crohn
disease.
•  Crohn disease most commonly affects the terminal ileum and cecum but can
involve any site within the GI tract. Disease can be discontinuous, resulting
in skip lesions, but pancolitis also occurs. In affected areas, disease usually
affects the full thickness of the entire bowel wall. Noncaseating granulomas
are common.
•  Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colonic mucosa and submucosa, is con-
tinuous from the rectum, and ranges from only rectal disease to pancolitis;
neither skip lesions nor granulomas are present.
•  IBD is thought to arise from a synergy between genetic risk, mucosal and
immune dysfunction, and dysbiosis (i.e., disease-associated changes in
microbial composition).
•  The risk of colonic epithelial dysplasia and adenocarcinoma is increased
in  IBD  patients  who  have  had  colonic  disease  for  more  than  8  to
10 years.
•  The two forms of microscopic colitis, collagenous colitis and lymphocytic
colitis, both cause chronic watery diarrhea. The intestines are endoscopically
normal, and the diseases are identified by their characteristic histologic
features.
•  Epithelial apoptosis is prominent in both graft-versus-host disease and
checkpoint inhibitor-induced colitis.
•  Irritable bowel syndrome is characterized by chronic, relapsing abdominal pain,
bloating, and changes in bowel habits without gross or histologic pathology.
The pathogenesis is not defined, but likely includes contributions by psycho-
logic stressors, diet, the gut microbiome, abnormal GI motility, and increased
enteric sensory responses to GI stimuli.

stood, but they are thought to result from decreased epithelial cell

nant potential. Their chief significance is that they must be distin-

important lesion.

Hyperplastic polyps are most commonly found in the left colon and are typically

these lesions (Fig. 17.44). Serration is typically restricted to the upper third of

jury and healing. Polyps that are part of the solitary rectal ulcer

charge, and an inflammatory lesion of the anterior rectal wall. The
underlying cause is impaired relaxation of the anorectal sphincter
that creates a sharp angle at the anterior rectal shelf and leads to
recurrent abrasion and ulceration of the overlying rectal mucosa.

lapse. The distinctive histologic features include mixed inflammatory

•  Crohn disease most commonly affects the terminal ileum and cecum but can involve any site within the GI tract. Disease can be discontinuous, resulting in skip lesions, but pancolitis also occurs. In affected areas, disease usually affects the full thickness of the entire bowel wall. Noncaseating granulomas are common.

•  Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colonic mucosa and submucosa, is continuous from the rectum, and ranges from only rectal disease to pancolitis; neither skip lesions nor granulomas are present.
•  IBD is thought to arise from a synergy between genetic risk, mucosal and immune dysfunction, and dysbiosis (i.e., disease-associated changes in microbial composition).
•  The risk of colonic epithelial dysplasia and adenocarcinoma is increased in  IBD  patients  who  have  had  colonic  disease  for  more  than  8  to
10 years.

•  The two forms of microscopic colitis, collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis, both cause chronic watery diarrhea. The intestines are endoscopically normal, and the diseases are identified by their characteristic histologic features.
•  Epithelial apoptosis is prominent in both graft-versus-host disease and checkpoint inhibitor-induced colitis.
•  Irritable bowel syndrome is characterized by chronic, relapsing abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits without gross or histologic pathology.
The pathogenesis is not defined, but likely includes contributions by psychologic stressors, diet, the gut microbiome, abnormal GI motility, and increased enteric sensory responses to GI stimuli.

•  Diverticular disease of the sigmoid colon is common in Western populations older than age 60 years. The causes include low-fiber diets, colonic spasm, and the unique anatomy of the colon. Inflammation of diverticula, diverticulitis, affects a minority of those with diverticulosis, but can cause perforation in its most severe form.
INTESTINAL POLYPS

Polyps are most common in the colon and rectum but, as discussed earlier, may occur in the esophagus, stomach, or small intestine. Most, if not all, polyps begin as small elevations of the mucosa. These are referred to as sessile, a term borrowed from botanists who use it to describe flowers and leaves that grow directly from the stem without a stalk. As sessile polyps enlarge, proliferation of cells adjacent to the mass and the effects of traction on the luminal protrusion may combine to create a stalk. Polyps with stalks are termed pedunculated. In general, intestinal polyps can be classified as nonneoplastic or neoplastic. The most common neoplastic polyp is the adenoma, which has the potential to progress to cancer. Nonneoplastic polyps can be classified as inflammatory, hamartomatous, or hyperplastic.
Hyperplastic Polyps

Colonic hyperplastic polyps are benign epithelial proliferations that are typically discovered in the sixth and seventh decades of life. The pathogenesis of hyperplastic polyps is incompletely understood, but they are thought to result from decreased epithelial cell turnover and delayed shedding of surface epithelial cells, leading to a

“piling up” of goblet and absorptive cells. These lesions have no malignant potential. Their chief significance is that they must be distinguished from sessile serrated polyps, which are histologically similar

but have malignant potential, as described later. It is also important to remember that epithelial hyperplasia can occur as a nonspecific reaction  adjacent  to  or  overlying  any  mass  or  inflammatory  lesion and therefore can be a clue to the presence of an adjacent, clinically important lesion.
MORPHOLOGY
Hyperplastic polyps are most commonly found in the left colon and are typically

less than 5 mm in diameter. They are smooth, nodular protrusions of the mucosa, often on the crests of mucosal folds. They may occur singly but are frequently multiple, particularly in the sigmoid colon and rectum. Histologically,

hyperplastic polyps are composed of mature goblet and absorptive cells with a serrated surface architecture that is the morphologic hallmark of these lesions (Fig. 17.44). Serration is typically restricted to the upper third of the crypt, and crypt base epithelium may have a regenerative appearance.
Inflammatory Polyps

Inflammatory polyps may form because of repeated cycles of injury and healing. Polyps that are part of the solitary rectal ulcer syndrome are an example of a purely inflammatory lesion. These patients present with a clinical triad of rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, and an inflammatory lesion of the anterior rectal wall. The underlying cause is impaired relaxation of the anorectal sphincter that creates a sharp angle at the anterior rectal shelf and leads to recurrent abrasion and ulceration of the overlying rectal mucosa.
Entrapment of this polyp in the fecal stream leads to mucosal prolapse. The distinctive histologic features include mixed inflammatory

Hamartomatous polyps occur sporadically or as components of
genetically determined or acquired syndromes ( Table 17.9 ). Although
they were originally thought to be developmental abnormalities, many
hamartomatous polyp syndromes are caused by germline mutations in

other intestinal or extraintestinal sites. Thus, a subset of hamartomatous

TABLE 17.9 Gastrointestinal Polyposis Syndromes
aAlso called PTEN hamartoma-tumor syndrome.
CNS, Central nervous system; FAP, familial adenomatous polyposis; GI, gastrointestinal; mTOR, mammalian (also called molecular) target of rapamycin; RPE, retinal
pigmented epithelium; TGF-β, transforming growth factor beta.
MORPHOLOGY
Most juvenile polyps are less than 3 cm in diameter. They are typically pedunculated, smooth-surfaced, reddish lesions with characteristic cystic spaces.
Microscopic examination shows these cysts to be dilated glands filled with
mucin and inflammatory debris (Fig. 17.46). The remainder of the polyp is
composed of lamina propria expanded by mixed inflammatory infiltrates. The
muscularis mucosae may be normal or attenuated.
Although the morphogenesis of juvenile polyps is incompletely
understood, it has been proposed that mucosal hyperplasia is the
initiating event. This hypothesis is consistent with the discovery that
mutations in pathways that regulate cellular growth cause autosomal
dominant juvenile polyposis. The most common mutation identified is
in SMAD4, which encodes a signaling intermediate in the TGF-β pathway. These patients often have both juvenile polyposis and hereditary
hemorrhagic telangiectasia. In other cases, mutations in BMPR1A,
which encodes a kinase that is a member of the TGF-β superfamily,
cause disease (see Table 17.9). Together these mutations account for
fewer than half of patients. Thus, other genes responsible for autosomal
dominant juvenile polyposis remain to be discovered.
Dysplasia is rare in sporadic juvenile polyps. In contrast, juvenile
polyposis syndrome is associated with dysplasia, both within the juvenile polyps and in separate adenomas. As a result, 30% to 50% of patients with juvenile polyposis develop colonic adenocarcinoma by age
45 years.
Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
This rare autosomal dominant syndrome presents at a median age of
11 years with multiple GI hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. The latter takes the form of dark blue to
brown macules on the lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, palmar surfaces of
the hands, genitalia, and perianal region. These lesions are similar to
freckles but are distinguished by their presence in the buccal mucosa.

Clinical Features
Because the morphology of Peutz-Jeghers polyps overlaps with that of
sporadic hamartomatous polyps, the presence of multiple polyps in the
small intestine, mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, and a positive family
history are critical to the diagnosis. Detection of STK11 mutations can be
helpful diagnostically in patients with polyps who lack mucocutaneous
hyperpigmentation. However, the absence of STK11 mutations does not
exclude the diagnosis, as these mutations are not present in all patients.
PREMALIGNANT AND MALIGNANT LESIONS
The most common neoplastic intestinal lesions are colonic adeno-
mas, which are polyps that are precursors to most colorectal adeno-
carcinomas. It is important, however, to realize that any mass lesion
within the gastrointestinal tract, including adenocarcinomas, neuroen-
docrine tumors, stromal tumors, lymphomas, and even metastases
from distant sites may form polyps. Although it accounts for 75% of
the overall length of the GI tract, tumors are relatively uncommon in
the small intestine. Among malignant small intestinal tumors, adeno-
carcinomas  and  well-differentiated  neuroendocrine  tumors  have
roughly equal incidence, followed by lymphomas and sarcomas.
Fig. 17.47 Peutz-Jeghers polyp. (A) Polyp surface (top) overlies stroma
composed of smooth muscle bundles cutting through the lamina propria.
(B) Complex glandular architecture and the presence of smooth muscle
are features that distinguish Peutz-Jeghers polyps from juvenile polyps.
Adenomas
Adenomas are epithelial neoplasms that range from small peduncu-
lated polyps to large sessile lesions. They develop in approximately
30% of adults living in the Western world by age 60 years. Colon ade-
nomas are less common in Asia, but their incidence has risen (in paral-
lel with increasing incidence of colorectal adenocarcinoma) as West-
ern diets and lifestyles become more prevalent. Because adenomas are
precursors to colorectal adenocarcinoma, surveillance colonoscopy is
recommended beginning at age 45 years. Individuals at increased risk,
including those with a family history of colorectal adenocarcinoma,
typically begin screening at least 10 years before the youngest age at
which a relative was diagnosed. Repeated surveillance colonoscopy is
both diagnostic and therapeutic, as polyps that have been removed
cannot become adenocarcinoma.
The prevalence of colorectal adenomas within populations correlates
with that of colorectal adenocarcinoma, and the distributions of adeno-
mas and adenocarcinoma within the colon are similar. Nevertheless, it
must be emphasized that most adenomas do not progress to become
adenocarcinomas.  There  are  no  tools  presently  available  to  identify
adenomas  that  are  destined  to  undergo  malignant  transformation.
Most adenomas are clinically silent, with the exception of large polyps
that can produce occult bleeding and anemia.

Clinical Features

Because the morphology of Peutz-Jeghers polyps overlaps with that of sporadic hamartomatous polyps, the presence of multiple polyps in the small intestine, mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, and a positive family history are critical to the diagnosis. Detection of STK11 mutations can be helpful diagnostically in patients with polyps who lack mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. However, the absence of STK11 mutations does not exclude the diagnosis, as these mutations are not present in all patients.
PREMALIGNANT AND MALIGNANT LESIONS

The most common neoplastic intestinal lesions are colonic adenomas, which are polyps that are precursors to most colorectal adenocarcinomas. It is important, however, to realize that any mass lesion within the gastrointestinal tract, including adenocarcinomas, neuroendocrine tumors, stromal tumors, lymphomas, and even metastases from distant sites may form polyps. Although it accounts for 75% of the overall length of the GI tract, tumors are relatively uncommon in the small intestine. Among malignant small intestinal tumors, adenocarcinomas  and  well-differentiated  neuroendocrine  tumors  have roughly equal incidence, followed by lymphomas and sarcomas.
Fig. 17.47 Peutz-Jeghers polyp. (A) Polyp surface (top) overlies stroma composed of smooth muscle bundles cutting through the lamina propria.
(B) Complex glandular architecture and the presence of smooth muscle are features that distinguish Peutz-Jeghers polyps from juvenile polyps.
Adenomas
Adenomas are epithelial neoplasms that range from small pedunculated polyps to large sessile lesions. They develop in approximately

30% of adults living in the Western world by age 60 years. Colon adenomas are less common in Asia, but their incidence has risen (in parallel with increasing incidence of colorectal adenocarcinoma) as Western diets and lifestyles become more prevalent. Because adenomas are

precursors to colorectal adenocarcinoma, surveillance colonoscopy is recommended beginning at age 45 years. Individuals at increased risk, including those with a family history of colorectal adenocarcinoma, typically begin screening at least 10 years before the youngest age at which a relative was diagnosed. Repeated surveillance colonoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic, as polyps that have been removed cannot become adenocarcinoma.

The prevalence of colorectal adenomas within populations correlates with that of colorectal adenocarcinoma, and the distributions of adenomas and adenocarcinoma within the colon are similar. Nevertheless, it must be emphasized that most adenomas do not progress to become adenocarcinomas.  There  are  no  tools  presently  available  to  identify adenomas  that  are  destined  to  undergo  malignant  transformation.
Most adenomas are clinically silent, with the exception of large polyps that can produce occult bleeding and anemia.

CHAPTER 17 The Gastrointestinal Tract 739
MORPHOLOGY
Colorectal adenomas are characterized by the presence of epithelial
dysplasia. Typical adenomas range from 0.3 to 10 cm in diameter and can
be pedunculated (Fig. 17.48A) or sessile, with the surface of both types having a texture resembling velvet or a raspberry (Fig. 17.48B). Histologically,
the hallmarks of epithelial dysplasia are nuclear hyperchromasia,
elongation, and stratification (Fig. 17.49C). These changes are most easily appreciated at the surface of the adenoma and are often accompanied by
prominent nucleoli, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a reduction in the number
of goblet cells. Pedunculated adenomas have slender fibromuscular stalks
(Fig. 17.48C) containing prominent blood vessels derived from the submucosa. The stalk is usually covered by nonneoplastic epithelium, but dysplasia
can be present.
Adenomas can be classified as tubular, tubulovillous, or villous based on
their architecture. These categories, however, have little clinical significance
in isolation. Tubular adenomas tend to be small, pedunculated polyps composed of rounded, or tubular, glands (Fig. 17.49A). In contrast, villous adenomas are covered by slender villi (Fig. 17.49B). Villous adenomas harbor cancers
more frequently than tubular adenomas, but this also correlates with larger
size. As the name implies, tubulovillous adenomas have a mixed architecture.
Sessile serrated polyps, also referred to as sessile serrated adenomas,
overlap histologically with hyperplastic polyps but are more commonly found
in the right colon. Despite their malignant potential, these polyps lack
typical cytologic features of dysplasia that are present in other adenomas. Histologically, these lesions can be differentiated from hyperplastic
polyps by the presence of serrated architecture throughout the full length
of the glands including the crypt base, crypt dilation, and lateral crypt extension (Fig. 17.49C).
Intramucosal carcinoma occurs when dysplastic epithelial cells breach the
basement membrane to invade the lamina propria. These may extend into, but
not through, the muscularis mucosae. Because functional lymphatic channels are
absent in the colonic mucosa, intramucosal carcinomas have little or no metastatic potential and complete polypectomy is generally curative (Fig. 17.50A).
Invasion beyond the muscularis mucosae (Fig. 17.50B), including into the submucosal stalk of a pedunculated polyp, constitutes invasive adenocarcinoma and
carries a risk of spread to other sites. In such cases, several factors, including
histologic grade of the invasive component, presence of vascular or lymphatic
invasion, and distance from the invasive component to the margin of resection
are considered in planning further therapy.
Although most colorectal adenomas are benign lesions, a small
proportion harbor invasive cancer at the time of detection. Size is the
most important characteristic that correlates with risk of malignancy. For example, while cancer is rare in adenomas less than 1 cm in
diameter, nearly 40% of lesions larger than 4 cm in diameter contain
foci of invasive cancer. High-grade dysplasia is also a risk factor for
cancer to an individual polyp but does not confer an increased risk of
cancer to other polyps within the same patient.
Adenocarcinoma of the colon is the most common malignancy of
the GI tract and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Before describing the pathogenesis and morphology of colon
cancer, we discuss two familial syndromes that have provided insight
into mechanisms of these tumors.
Familial Adenomatous Polyposis
Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant
disorder in which patients develop numerous colorectal adenomas as teenagers. It is caused by germline mutation of the adenomatous polyposis coli, or APC, gene, which is a key negative regulator of the Wnt signaling pathway (Chapter 7). Approximately 75% of
cases are inherited, while the remainder appear to be caused by de
novo mutations.
At least 100 polyps are necessary for a diagnosis of classic FAP, but
thousands may be present (Fig. 17.51). Except for their numbers, FAP-associated polyps are morphologically indistinguishable from sporadic
adenomas. However, flat or depressed adenomas are also prevalent in
FAP, and microscopic adenomas, consisting of only one or two dysplastic
crypts, occur in otherwise normal-appearing mucosa.
Colorectal adenocarcinoma develops in 100% of untreated FAP
patients, often before age 30 years and nearly always by age 50 years.
As a result, prophylactic colectomy is the standard of care. Colectomy
prevents colorectal cancer, but patients remain at risk for neoplasia at
other sites. The ampulla of Vater and the stomach are common extra-colonic sites of adenomas, and, if untreated, cancer, in FAP patients.
FAP is associated with a variety of extraintestinal manifestations
including congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium,
which can be detected at birth and may be an adjunct to early screening. Specific APC mutations have been associated with other manifestations of FAP and partly explain variants such as Gardner syndrome
and Turcot syndrome (Table 17.10).
Fig. 17.48 Colonic adenomas. (A) Pedunculated adenoma (endoscopic view). (B) Adenoma with a velvety
surface. (C) Low-magnification photomicrograph of a pedunculated tubular adenoma.

It is caused by germline mutation of the adenomatous polyposis coli, or APC, gene, which is a key negative regulator of the Wnt signaling pathway (Chapter 7). Approximately 75% of cases are inherited, while the remainder appear to be caused by de novo mutations.

At least 100 polyps are necessary for a diagnosis of classic FAP, but thousands may be present (Fig. 17.51). Except for their numbers, FAP-associated polyps are morphologically indistinguishable from sporadic adenomas. However, flat or depressed adenomas are also prevalent in FAP, and microscopic adenomas, consisting of only one or two dysplastic crypts, occur in otherwise normal-appearing mucosa.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma develops in 100% of untreated FAP patients, often before age 30 years and nearly always by age 50 years. As a result, prophylactic colectomy is the standard of care. Colectomy prevents colorectal cancer, but patients remain at risk for neoplasia at other sites. The ampulla of Vater and the stomach are common extra-colonic sites of adenomas, and, if untreated, cancer, in FAP patients. FAP is associated with a variety of extraintestinal manifestations including congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, which can be detected at birth and may be an adjunct to early screening. Specific APC mutations have been associated with other manifestations of FAP and partly explain variants such as Gardner syndrome and Turcot syndrome (Table 17.10).

MORPHOLOGY

Colorectal adenomas are characterized by the presence of epithelial dysplasia. Typical adenomas range from 0.3 to 10 cm in diameter and can be pedunculated (Fig. 17.48A) or sessile, with the surface of both types having a texture resembling velvet or a raspberry (Fig. 17.48B). Histologically, the hallmarks of epithelial dysplasia are nuclear hyperchromasia, elongation, and stratification (Fig. 17.49C). These changes are most easily appreciated at the surface of the adenoma and are often accompanied by prominent nucleoli, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a reduction in the number of goblet cells. Pedunculated adenomas have slender fibromuscular stalks (Fig. 17.48C) containing prominent blood vessels derived from the submucosa. The stalk is usually covered by nonneoplastic epithelium, but dysplasia can be present.

Adenomas can be classified as tubular, tubulovillous, or villous based on their architecture. These categories, however, have little clinical significance in isolation. Tubular adenomas tend to be small, pedunculated polyps composed of rounded, or tubular, glands (Fig. 17.49A). In contrast, villous adenomas are covered by slender villi (Fig. 17.49B). Villous adenomas harbor cancers more frequently than tubular adenomas, but this also correlates with larger size. As the name implies, tubulovillous adenomas have a mixed architecture. Sessile serrated polyps, also referred to as sessile serrated adenomas, overlap histologically with hyperplastic polyps but are more commonly found in the right colon. Despite their malignant potential, these polyps lack typical cytologic features of dysplasia that are present in other adenomas. Histologically, these lesions can be differentiated from hyperplastic polyps by the presence of serrated architecture throughout the full length of the glands including the crypt base, crypt dilation, and lateral crypt extension (Fig. 17.49C). Intramucosal carcinoma occurs when dysplastic epithelial cells breach the basement membrane to invade the lamina propria. These may extend into, but not through, the muscularis mucosae. Because functional lymphatic channels are absent in the colonic mucosa, intramucosal carcinomas have little or no metastatic potential and complete polypectomy is generally curative (Fig. 17.50A). Invasion beyond the muscularis mucosae (Fig. 17.50B), including into the submucosal stalk of a pedunculated polyp, constitutes invasive adenocarcinoma and carries a risk of spread to other sites. In such cases, several factors, including histologic grade of the invasive component, presence of vascular or lymphatic invasion, and distance from the invasive component to the margin of resection are considered in planning further therapy.

Although most colorectal adenomas are benign lesions, a small proportion harbor invasive cancer at the time of detection. Size is the most important characteristic that correlates with risk of malignancy. For example, while cancer is rare in adenomas less than 1 cm in diameter, nearly 40% of lesions larger than 4 cm in diameter contain foci of invasive cancer. High-grade dysplasia is also a risk factor for cancer to an individual polyp but does not confer an increased risk of cancer to other polyps within the same patient.

Adenocarcinoma of the colon is the most common malignancy of the GI tract and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Before describing the pathogenesis and morphology of colon cancer, we discuss two familial syndromes that have provided insight into mechanisms of these tumors.
